title: Opinions, TV series and authentic listening

blocks.text: The last unit of the Egyptian track takes you out of the built dialogues: learn to say what you think (ana šāyif Inn..., fi raʾyi...), whether or not to agree with the vivacity typical of an Egyptian discussion (laʾ ṭabʿan!, maʿāk miyya fi l-miyya), to talk about television series and movies, and above all to listen to the real Egyptian: fast, full of words that fill (yaʿni, ʾaṣdi, i-muhimm), contractions and jokes. Egyptian series and films are known all over the Arab world: they are also the most pleasant way to continue learning after this volume. Seven weeks, in parallel with INT-01INT-02, the Test B1.4 and B1-24.

rows: 10–11 hours · seven weeks (weeks 149–155), about 1,5 hours per week in two blocks

blocks.text: Materials This unit, a tutor or Egyptian conversation partner, an Egyptian series or film with Arabic subtitles (Appendix C)
Targets. At the end of the unit you know:
1. express and motivate an opinion in Egyptian, and agree or disagree with gradations;
2. tell the plot of a movie or episode and say what you liked and what not;
3. recognizing and using the main words-signal of speech (yaʿni, ʾaṣdi, ʿala fikra, il-muhimm, ṭab, bass);
4. to understand the quick Egyptian in its most frequent phenomena (contractions, vocal falls, short forms);
5. follow an authentic scene of a series with a method in four stages.
Seven-week plan (two blocks from 40–45 minutes per week).

In the quick talk of the series many words are shortened. Recognizing these forms is half of the work.

ana miš ʿārif maʿrafš I don't know. Other phenomena. Short vowels that are not accented fall: kitīr → ktīr, simiʿt → smiʿt. The ḥa- of the future often becomes ha-. Foreign words are everywhere (mobāyl, laptop, uber, story): it's not a problem, it's contemporary Egyptian.

What to choose. To begin with: a recent Egyptian series or film, with subtitles in Arabic (not in English), and scenes of daily dialogue (family, friends, work). Classic black and white films (the 1950s and 1960s, with actresses and actors like Fātin Ḥamāma) have a slower and clearer Egyptian, and are still very loved. See Appendix C for platforms and resources. The method in four stages (for a scene of 2–3 minutes).
1. Look without stopping, with Arab subtitles. Who am I, where am I, what's going on? Write three words
key.
2. Look again, sentence by sentence. Stop after every line, read the subtitle, repeat aloud. Note the
new words and words-signal (section 5).
3. Look without subtitles. Now you understand more: mark in percentage how much (like Luke: 70% with 50%
without).
4. Shadowing and summarized. Repeat three lines imitating rhythm and intonation; then tells the scene in Egyptian in
One minute. How much? One scene a day, fifteen minutes, is worth more than one whole movie once a month. It's about the same scene after a week: you'll see how much better listening has been.

The emphasis on opinion. In Egyptian the emphasis is placed stretching and raising the voice on the important word: from ḥilw ʾaaawi! · laʾ ṭabʿaaan! · miyya fi l-miyya! Imitates the tutor: it is part of the meaning. The rhetorical questions. izzāy yaʿni?! What would it be like?!! and mumill?! They are said with a very high pitch and then comes down suddenly: it is astonishment, not a real question.
